label: introthm:discretization
title: \textquotedblleft Theorem\textquotedblright
body_md:
\label{introthm:discretization}
Let $H$ be a regulated, $\sigma$-sparse Hermitian family on $[0,T]$, with evolution $U$ starting at the identity. If its entrywise $k$-bit truncation $H^{(k)}$ is piecewise constant, the induced product $W$, one exponential per constant piece, satisfies
\[
 \|W-U(T)\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma 2^{-k}T.
\]
head: environment

label: introthm:fine-count
title: \textquotedblleft Theorem\textquotedblright
body_md:
\label{introthm:fine-count}
For a regulated, $\sigma$-sparse Hermitian family $H$ on $[0,T]$ with total variation $0<\ell<\infty$, holding truncated midpoint samples between equal-variation checkpoints gives a product within $\varepsilon$ of $U(T)$, with $O(T\ell/\varepsilon)$ factors and $O(\log_2(\sigma T/\varepsilon))$ bits as $\varepsilon\to0$.
head: environment

label: introthm:unit
title: \textquotedblleft Theorem\textquotedblright
body_md:
\label{introthm:unit}
For integer $T\ge1$, let $H$ be a twice continuously differentiable Hermitian family on $[0,1]$ with $\|H'\|\leL$ and $\|H''\|\le2\nu$, $U$ its evolution under $H(t/T)$ starting at the identity, and $W_T=e^{-iH((T-1)/T)}\cdots e^{-iH(1/T)}e^{-iH(0)}$. Suppose each interior sample $H(j/T)$, $0<j<T$, has spectrum in an interval of length at most $\barw$, and its nonzero eigenvalue differences lie at distance at least $\gamma>0$ from every nonzero multiple of $2\pi$, with $L$, $\nu$, $\gamma$, and $\barw$ independent of $T$. Then
\[
 \bigl\|e^{-iH(1)/2}W_Te^{iH(0)/2}-U(T)\bigr\|=O_{\gamma,\barw}\bigl((L+L^2+\nu)/T\bigr).
\]

label: def:regulated
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:regulated}
A map $H$ from $[0,T]$ to the $d\times d$ matrices is \emph{regulated} if it
has a limit from the right at every $t\in[0,T)$ and a limit from the left at
every $t\in(0,T]$.
head: environment

label: lem:duhamel
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $t\in[a,b]\setminus S$, the product rule and the two evolution equations give
$\frac{d}{dt}(U^{\dagger}V)=i\,U^{\dagger}(H-G)V$,
whose norm is $\|H-G\|$ by unitarity. The fundamental theorem of calculus for a
continuous function with integrable derivative outside a countable set
(see \cite[(8.7.1)--(8.7.2)]{dieudonne1960} for regulated derivatives) gives
\[
  U(b)^\daggerV(b)-1
  =i\int_a^bU(t)^\dagger\bigl(H(t)-G(t)\bigr)V(t)\,dt,
\]
since $U(a)^\daggerV(a)=1$. Taking norms, using the integral triangle inequality
and unitary invariance of the norm, gives \eqref{eq:duhamel-integral}.
head: environment

label: prop:regulated-evolution
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:regulated-evolution}
Every regulated family $H\colon[0,T]\to\mathbb C^{d\times d}$ is bounded
and has at most countably many discontinuities, hence a set of discontinuities of measure zero.
It has a unique continuous unitary evolution $U$, with $U(0)=1$, satisfying
\[
  U(t)=1-i\int_0^tH(s)U(s)\,ds.
\]
At every continuity point of $H$, $i\dotU(t)=H(t)U(t)$,
with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. In particular, $U$ satisfies the equation at all but
countably many times.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose piecewise-constant Hermitian $H_n\toH$ uniformly, each equal to $H$ at its piece endpoints \cite[(7.6.1)]{dieudonne1960}.
Uniform convergence makes $H$ bounded and continuous outside the countable union of partition points.
Their unitary evolutions $U_n$ satisfy
$\sup_t\|U_n(t)-U_m(t)\|\le T\sup_t\|H_n(t)-H_m(t)\|$ by \Cref{lem:duhamel}, so they converge uniformly to a continuous unitary $U$ with $U(0)=1$.
Passing to the limit in
$U_n(t)=1-i\int_0^tH_n(s)U_n(s)\,ds$ gives the integral equation, since the integrands converge uniformly.
At continuity points of $H$, the integrand $H(s)U(s)$ is continuous, so the fundamental theorem of calculus gives the stated derivatives.
Finally, \Cref{lem:duhamel} with identical generators gives uniqueness.
head: environment

label: def:spectral-window
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:spectral-window}
For a Hermitian matrix $H$ and a compact interval $I$, the \emph{spectral
projector} $P_I(H)$ projects orthogonally onto the span of the eigenvectors
of $H$ with eigenvalues in $I$. For $\Gamma>0$, $H$ has a \emph{gap $\Gamma$
around $I$} if every eigenvalue of $H$ outside $I$ lies at distance at least
$\Gamma$ from $I$, and $I^{+}$ is $I$ extended by $\Gamma/2$ at each end. The
\emph{leakage} of a matrix $X$ from a projector $P$ to a projector $Q$ is
$\|(1-Q)XP\|$.
head: environment

label: thm:davis-kahan
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:davis-kahan}
Let $H,G\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$ be Hermitian, let $I,J$ be compact intervals, and
suppose every eigenvalue of $G$ outside $J$ lies at distance at least $\Gamma>0$
from $I$. Then
\[
  \bigl\|(1-P_J(G))\,P_I(H)\bigr\|
  \le\frac{\bigl\|(1-P_J(G))(H-G)P_I(H)\bigr\|}{\Gamma}
  \le\frac{\|H-G\|}{\Gamma} .
\]
head: environment
name: Davis--Kahan, $\sin\Theta$

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $m,c$ be the midpoint and half-width of $I$, and put $P=P_I(H)$ and $Q=1-P_J(G)$.
The spectral hypotheses give $\|(H-m1)P\|\le c$ and $\|(G-m1)Qv\|\ge(c+\Gamma)\|Qv\|$.
Since $P$ commutes with $H$ and $Q$ with $G$, for every unit vector $v$,
\[
 (c+\Gamma)\|QPv\|\le\|(G-m1)QPv\|
 =\|QP(H-m1)Pv+Q(G-H)Pv\|
 \le c\|QP\|+\|Q(G-H)P\|.
\]
Taking the supremum over $v$ and subtracting $c\|QP\|$ gives the first inequality,
and projector contraction gives the second.
head: environment

label: def:exponential-operators
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:exponential-operators}
For a matrix $H$, the \emph{averaging operator} is
\[
  \Phi_H(E)=\int_0^1 e^{i\tau H}Ee^{-i\tau H}\,d\tau ,
\]
and the commutator map is $a_H(E)=i(H E-EH)$.
The \emph{spectral width} of $H$ is the length of the smallest interval
containing its eigenvalues. Write $B_n$ for the Bernoulli numbers, with $B_1=-\frac12$.
For $0\lew<2\pi$ and $x\notin2\pi\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$, put
\[
  \mathcal B(w)=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{|B_n|}{n!}w^n ,\qquad
  \mathcal N(x)=\frac{1-\frac x2\cot\frac x2}{x^2},\qquad \mathcal N(0)=\tfrac1{12}.
\]
For $H$ with no eigenvalue difference in $2\pi\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$, the \emph{frame operator} $\Theta_H$
multiplies the $(p,q)$ entry of a matrix, written in an eigenbasis of $H$ with
eigenvalues $\lambda_p$, by $\mathcal N(\lambda_p-\lambda_q)$.
For $\gamma>0$, a Hermitian matrix is \emph{$\gamma$-separated} if each of its eigenvalue differences $x$ satisfies
$x=0$ or $|x-2\pi n|\ge\gamma$ for every nonzero integer $n$.
head: environment

label: lem:bernoulli-inverse
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:bernoulli-inverse}
Let $h,\tilde h$ be Hermitian.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Suppose that $\gamma>0$ and $h,\tilde h$ are $\gamma$-separated of spectral width at most $\barw$. The frame operator $\Theta_h$ preserves Hermitian matrices and, for every matrix $D$, solves
\begin{equation}\label{eq:frame}
  e^{ih}\,\Theta_h(D)\,e^{-ih}-\Theta_h(D)
  =\int_0^1\bigl(\tau-\tfrac12\bigr)\,e^{i\tau h}De^{-i\tau h}\,d\tau .
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\[
 \|\Theta_h\|\le N_\gamma,\qquad
 \|\Theta_h-\Theta_{\tilde h}\|\le N'_\gamma\|h-\tilde h\|,
\]
with dimension-independent constants depending only on $\gamma$ and $\barw$.
\item If $h,\tilde h$ have spectral width at most $w<2\pi$, they are $\gamma'$-separated for every $0<\gamma'\le2\pi-w$.
In this case, the frame-operator bounds hold with $\mathcal N(w)$ and $2\mathcal N'(w)$ in place of $N_\gamma$ and $N'_\gamma$.
\item If $h,\tilde h$ have spectral width at most $w<2\pi$, the inverse averaging operator used for walks is
\[
 \Phi_h^{-1}=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{B_n}{n!}\,a_h^{\,n}.
\]
It preserves Hermitian matrices, with
\[
 \|\Phi_h^{-1}\|\le\mathcal B(w),\qquad
 \|\Phi_h^{-1}-\Phi_{\tilde h}^{-1}\|\le2\mathcal B'(w)\|h-\tilde h\|.
\]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In an eigenbasis of $h$, let $x=\lambda_p-\lambda_q$. Comparing the multipliers of $D_{pq}$ reduces \eqref{eq:frame} to
\[
 (e^{ix}-1)\mathcal N(x)=\int_0^1\bigl(\tau-\tfrac12\bigr)e^{i\tau x}\,d\tau .
\]
Both sides vanish at $x=0$. For $x\notin2\pi\mathbb Z$,
\begin{align*}
 (e^{ix}-1)\mathcal N(x)
 &=\frac{e^{ix}-1}{x^2}+\frac{e^{ix}+1}{2ix} &&\text{since }\cot\tfrac x2=\tfrac{i(e^{ix}+1)}{e^{ix}-1},\\
 &=\int_0^1\bigl(\tau-\tfrac12\bigr)e^{i\tau x}\,d\tau &&\text{integrating by parts}.
\end{align*}

Since $\mathcal N$ is real and even, the frame preserves Hermitian matrices entrywise.
The eigenvalue differences allowed by $\gamma$-separation and width at most $\barw$ form a compact set avoiding the poles. Choose a smooth compactly supported cutoff $\chi=1$ there, supported away from the poles, and let $g$ be the Fourier transform of the smooth extension $\chi\mathcal N$.
Fourier inversion gives $\Theta_h(D)=\int_{\mathbb R}g(s)e^{2\pi ish}De^{-2\pi ish}\,ds$, so unitary invariance gives $N_\gamma=\|g\|_1$. Duhamel bounds $\|e^{2\pi ish}-e^{2\pi is\tilde h}\|$ by $2\pi|s|\,\|h-\tilde h\|$ on each side of $D$, giving $N'_\gamma=4\pi\int_{\mathbb R}|s g(s)|\,ds$, finite because $g$ decays faster than any power.

If $|x|\lew<2\pi$ and $n\ne0$, then $|x-2\pi n|\ge2\pi|n|-|x|\ge2\pi-w$.
For (2)--(3), $\|a_h\|\lew<2\pi$, and since a scalar shift of
$h$ preserves $a_h$ and gives $\|h\|\lew/2<\pi$, the inverse
formula follows from \cite[Lemma~3]{blanes2009} applied to $ih$.

For the explicit bounds of (2), since $|x|\lew<2\pi$, the convergent series $\sum_{n\ge0}B_{n+2}a_h^{\,n}/(n+2)!$ multiplies entry $(p,q)$ by
$(z/(e^z-1)-1+z/2)/z^2$ at $z=ix$, which is $\mathcal N(x)$ because
$z/(e^z-1)+z/2=(z/2)\coth(z/2)$, $(ix/2)\coth(ix/2)=(x/2)\cot(x/2)$, and $z^2=-x^2$. So this series is $\Theta_h$, and $\mathcal N(x)=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^mB_{2m+2}x^{2m}/(2m+2)!$, since odd Bernoulli numbers past $B_1$ vanish.

Since $\|a_h^{\,n}\|\lew^n$ and $(-1)^mB_{2m+2}=|B_{2m+2}|$, the absolute coefficient sums bound the operator norms by $\mathcal B(w)$ and $\mathcal N(w)$.
Telescoping powers with $\|i[h-\tilde h,E]\|\le2\|h-\tilde h\|\|E\|$ gives
$\|a_h^{\,n}-a_{\tilde h}^{\,n}\|\le nw^{n-1}\|a_h-a_{\tilde h}\|
\le2nw^{n-1}\|h-\tilde h\|$ for $n\ge1$. Termwise differentiation of the majorants
then gives the Lipschitz bounds. Both series preserve Hermitian matrices, since their
coefficients are real and $a_h$ preserves Hermiticity.
head: environment

label: rem:alias
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:alias}
Separation is a sampling condition on step length times eigenvalue differences.
At an eigenvalue difference $x=2\pi n\ne0$, the averaging multiplier $(e^{ix}-1)/(ix)$ vanishes, so the exponential derivative is not invertible. In \eqref{eq:frame}, the left multiplier $e^{ix}-1$ vanishes, while integration by parts gives $1/(2\pi in)$ on the right, so a nonzero entry of $D$ at that difference prevents a solution.
A walk must choose its logarithm (\Cref{sec:walks}), since for an orthogonal projector $P$ commuting with $H$,
$e^{-i(H+2\pi P)}=e^{-iH}e^{-2\pi iP}=e^{-iH}$ by $e^{-2\pi iP}=1+(e^{-2\pi i}-1)P=1$.

label: def:truncation
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:truncation}
Let $k$ be any integer. The \emph{truncation at scale $2^{-k}$} of a real number $x$
rounds its magnitude down to a multiple of $2^{-k}$ and restores its sign:
\[
  [x]_k=2^{-k}\operatorname{trunc}(2^k x),
\]
where $\operatorname{trunc}(y)$ removes the fractional part of $y$, rounding toward zero.
A complex number is truncated in its real and imaginary parts,
$[z]_k=[\operatorname{Re}z]_k+i[\operatorname{Im}z]_k$. A matrix $H$ is truncated entry
by entry, $H^{(k)}_{pq}=[H_{pq}]_k$, and a family pointwise,
$H^{(k)}(t)=H(t)^{(k)}$.
For nonnegative $k$, this is $k$-bit truncation.
head: environment
name: Bit truncation

label: lem:units
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:units}
Let $j$ be a nonnegative integer. The family $t\mapsto2^jH(2^jt)$ on $[0,2^{-j}T]$ has
evolution $t\mapstoU(2^jt)$, which equals $U(T)$ at time $2^{-j}T$. Moreover,
$[2^jx]_k=2^j[x]_{k+j}$ for every real $x$ and nonnegative integer $k$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the chain rule, $i\frac{d}{dt}U(2^jt)=2^jH(2^jt)U(2^jt)$ wherever $U$ is
differentiable at $2^jt$, which is at all but countably many $t$. The initial value is $U(0)=1$, so \Cref{lem:duhamel} with identical generators gives uniqueness. For the second claim, the definition of truncation gives
$[2^jx]_k=2^{-k}\operatorname{trunc}(2^{k+j}x)=2^j[x]_{k+j}$.
head: environment

label: lem:truncation-error
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $t$ and suppress it. Truncation preserves Hermiticity and zeros, so
$H-H^{(k)}$ is Hermitian with at most $\sigma$ nonzero entries in each row.
The real and imaginary parts of each entry have truncation errors below $2^{-k}$, so each entry has modulus less than $\sqrt2\,2^{-k}$. The row-sum bound for Hermitian matrices therefore gives
\[
  \bigl\|H-H^{(k)}\bigr\|\le\max_p\sum_q\bigl|H_{pq}-[H_{pq}]_k\bigr|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k}.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:induced
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:induced}
Let $H$ be regulated and $\sigma$-sparse, with evolution $U$, and let $k$ be a
nonnegative integer. If $H^{(k)}$ is regulated, its evolution $V$ satisfies
\[
  \|V(t)-U(t)\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k}t
  \qquad(0\le t\le T).
\]
In particular, whenever $H^{(k)}$ is piecewise constant, its induced product
$W=V(T)$ (\Cref{def:piecewise}) satisfies
$\|W-U(T)\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k}T$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Truncation preserves Hermiticity, so \Cref{prop:regulated-evolution} gives both evolutions,
with $U(0)=V(0)=1$. By \Cref{lem:truncation-error},
$\|H(s)-H^{(k)}(s)\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k}$ for $s\in[0,T]$.
Applying \Cref{lem:duhamel} outside both countable exceptional sets and the endpoints
and integrating over $[0,t]$ gives $\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k}t$.
For piecewise-constant truncation, gluing constant-generator evolutions gives
$V(T)=W$, one exponential per piece (\Cref{def:piecewise}), and we take $t=T$.
head: environment

label: def:variation-checkpoints
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:variation-checkpoints}
We measure how
much $H$ changes by its total variation up to time $t$,
\[
  \ell(t)=\sup\sum_{r}\bigl\|H(s_{r+1})-H(s_r)\bigr\|,
\]
the supremum over partitions $0=s_0<s_1<\dots<s_m=t$, and write $\ell=\ell(T)$.
We define \emph{checkpoints} as any nondecreasing list of times $0=t_0\le\dots\le t_n=T$.
head: environment

label: lem:inverse-levels
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:inverse-levels}
Suppose $\ell<\infty$, and let $n\ge1$ be an integer. Set $t_0=0$, $t_n=T$, and
\[
  t_j=\inf\bigl\{t\in[0,T]:\ell(t)\ge j\ell/n\bigr\}
  \qquad(0<j<n).
\]
These equal-variation checkpoints are nondecreasing, and on each interval the variation stays between two
consecutive levels: for $t_j<x\le y<t_{j+1}$,
\[
  j\ell/n\le\ell(x)\le\ell(y)\le(j+1)\ell/n,
\]
so that $\|H(y)-H(x)\|\le\ell/n$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The sets defining the infima contain $T$ and shrink as $j$ increases, so their infima are nondecreasing.
For $j>0$, $x>t_j$ puts a point of the $j$th set below $x$,
and for $j+1<n$, $y<t_{j+1}$ keeps $y$ outside the next set, so
monotonicity gives the displayed bounds, with endpoint cases given by $0\le\ell(t)\le\ell$.
Subtracting gives $\|H(y)-H(x)\|\le\ell(y)-\ell(x)\le\ell/n$.
head: environment

label: def:midpoint-product
title: Definition
head: environment

label: lem:main
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:main}
Let $H$ be $\sigma$-sparse and write $U$ for its evolution, which exists in each case below (\Cref{prop:regulated-evolution}). Let
$0<\varepsilon\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,T$, and let $k$ be
the least nonnegative integer with $2^k\ge\sqrt2\,\sigma\,T/\varepsilon$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $H$ is regulated, there are checkpoints whose midpoint product $W$ (\Cref{def:midpoint-product}) satisfies
\(
  \|W-U(T)\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k}T\le\varepsilon.
\)
\item (Equal-variation steps.) If $0<\ell<\infty$, $W$ satisfies the same bound for
$n=\lceil2^{k+1}\ell/(\sqrt2\,\sigma)\rceil$ and the checkpoints of
\Cref{lem:inverse-levels}, and $n\le1+4T\ell/\varepsilon$.
\item (Uniform steps \cite{dam2001}.) If $L>0$ and $\|H(t)-H(u)\|\leL\,|t-u|$, $W$ satisfies the same bound for
$t_j=jT/n$ with $n=\lceil2^{k+1}L T/(\sqrt2\,\sigma)\rceil$, and
$n\le1+4L T^2/\varepsilon$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In (1), take a step approximation within
$\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k-2}$ of $H$ \cite[(7.6.1)]{dieudonne1960}, with its piece endpoints
as checkpoints. The triangle inequality through its constant value bounds each open piece's oscillation by
$\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k-1}$.
In (2), \Cref{lem:inverse-levels} bounds it by
$\ell/n\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k-1}$, and in (3), the Lipschitz bound on length $T/n$ gives
$L T/n\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k-1}$, both by the ceilings, which are positive since $\ell,L T>0$.

For $t_j<t<t_{j+1}$, the triangle inequality through the midpoint sample
$H\bigl(\tfrac{t_j+t_{j+1}}2\bigr)$ and
\Cref{lem:truncation-error} at $k+1$ bits give
\[
  \|H(t)-G_j\|
  \le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k-1}+\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k-1}
  =\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k}.
\]
Since $W$ is generated piecewise by $G_j$, \Cref{lem:duhamel} and the choice of $k$ give
$\|W-U(T)\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k}T\le\varepsilon$.

For $k>0$, minimality gives
$\varepsilon\,2^{k-1}<\sqrt2\,\sigma\,T$, hence
$2^{k+1}/(\sqrt2\,\sigma)\le4T/\varepsilon$, and for $k=0$, the same bound follows from
$\varepsilon\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,T$. The ceiling bound
$\lceil x\rceil\le x+1$ then gives both counts.

label: lem:transfer
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:transfer}
Let $H_0$ and $H_T$ have a gap $\Gamma>0$ around intervals
$I$ and $J$, respectively, and let $D_0$ and $D_T$ be Hermitian with
$\|H_0-D_0\|,\|H_T-D_T\|\le\eta'$. Write $P$ and $Q$ for the
spectral projectors of $H_0$ for $I$ and of $H_T$ for $J$, and $P'$
and $Q'$ for those of $D_0$ for $I^{+}$ and of $D_T$ for $J^{+}$. Then for every
matrix $X$ of norm at most one and every matrix $Y$,
\[
  \bigl\|(1-Q')YP'-(1-Q)XP\bigr\|\le\|Y-X\|+\frac{4\eta'}{\Gamma}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $I^+$ widens $I$ by $\Gamma/2$, eigenvalues of $D_0$ outside $I^+$ are more than $\Gamma/2$ from $I$.
The gap separates eigenvalues of $H_0$ outside $I$ from $I^+$ by at least $\Gamma-\Gamma/2=\Gamma/2$.
Thus, \Cref{thm:davis-kahan} in both directions, with gap $\Gamma/2$, bounds
$\|(1-P')P\|$ and $\|(1-P)P'\|$ by $2\|H_0-D_0\|/\Gamma$.
Their maximum is $\|P-P'\|$, since $P-P'$ is Hermitian and
$(P-P')^2=P(1-P')P+(1-P)P'(1-P)$ is block diagonal on
$\operatorname{ran}P\oplus\ker P$, with block norms $\|(1-P')P\|^2$ and $\|(1-P)P'\|^2$.
Hence, $\|P-P'\|\le2\eta'/\Gamma$ by the endpoint error bound. The same argument at $T$
gives $\|Q-Q'\|\le2\eta'/\Gamma$.

Adding and subtracting $(1-Q')XP$ and $(1-Q')XP'$ gives
\[
  (1-Q')YP'-(1-Q)XP
  =(Q-Q')XP+(1-Q')(Y-X)P'+(1-Q')X(P'-P).
\]
Since $X$ and the orthogonal projectors are contractions, the triangle inequality and
submultiplicativity bound its norm by
$\|Q-Q'\|+\|Y-X\|+\|P'-P\|\le\|Y-X\|+4\eta'/\Gamma$.
head: environment

label: rem:gap
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:gap}
The gap $\Gamma$ enters \Cref{lem:transfer} only through the replacement of $H_0$ and
$H_T$ by $D_0$ and $D_T$. Any other perturbation bound for the endpoint projectors can replace Davis--Kahan, and it
then decides how, if at all, a gap appears. Since
the intervals $I$ and $J$ are chosen independently, the eigenvalues followed may even shift in energy between
the ends.
head: environment

label: thm:transfer
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:transfer}
Let $H$ be regulated and $\sigma$-sparse, and let $k$ be a nonnegative integer.
Let $W$ be either
\begin{enumerate}
\item the induced product of a piecewise-constant truncation $H^{(k)}$ (\Cref{lem:induced}), or
\item a midpoint product of \Cref{lem:main} at some accuracy $\varepsilon$, with $k$ chosen for that accuracy and $(k+1)$-bit generators.
\end{enumerate}
Let $H(0)$ and $H(T)$ have gaps $\Gamma$ around $I$ and $J$, put $P=P_I(H(0))$ and
$Q=P_J(H(T))$, and let $P'$ and $Q'$ be the spectral projectors of the $k$-bit endpoint truncations
$H^{(k)}(0)$ for $I^{+}$ and $H^{(k)}(T)$ for $J^{+}$. In either case,
\[
  \bigl\|(1-Q')WP'-(1-Q)U(T)P\bigr\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k}(T+4/\Gamma).
\]
Moreover, $\|(1-S)(W-U(T))R\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k}T$ for arbitrary orthogonal projectors $R,S$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \Cref{lem:induced} or \Cref{lem:main}, $\|W-U(T)\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k}T$,
so, by \Cref{lem:truncation-error}, \Cref{lem:transfer} applies with Hermitian $D_0=H^{(k)}(0)$,
$D_T=H^{(k)}(T)$, unitary $X=U(T)$, $Y=W$, and $\eta'=\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k}$.
For orthogonal projectors $R,S$, contractivity gives $\|(1-S)(W-U(T))R\|\le\|W-U(T)\|$.
head: environment

label: def:continuous-discrete-leakage
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:continuous-discrete-leakage}
When $H(0)$ and $H(T)$ have a gap $\Gamma$ around intervals $I$ and $J$, respectively, we define the \emph{continuous leakage} as the leakage of
$U(T)$ from $P_I(H(0))$ to $P_J(H(T))$. For a product $W$ and precision $k$, we define the
\emph{discrete leakage} as the leakage of $W$ from $P_{I^+}(H^{(k)}(0))$ to $P_{J^+}(H^{(k)}(T))$.

\Cref{thm:transfer} gives convergence of the leakages, while the proof of \Cref{lem:transfer} gives

label: cor:jrs
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:jrs}
Let $\tildeH$ be $\sigma$-sparse and twice continuously
differentiable on an open interval containing $[0,1]$. Let $\tildeH(s)$ have a band
of $m$ eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, isolated from the rest of its spectrum by a gap
$g(s)>0$, as in \cite[Theorem~3]{jansen2007}, and let $P$ and $Q$ be the band's spectral projectors at $s=0$ and $s=1$. Put
$C=J_m(\|\tildeH'\|,\|\tildeH''\|,g)$, and let $\ell$ be the total variation of $\tildeH$ on $[0,1]$. Suppose that $C$ and $\ell$ are positive, and let
$H(t)=\tildeH(t/T)$. Assume the continuous bound $\|(1-Q)U(T)P\|\le C/T$ of that theorem, and suppose that $C\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,T^2$. Let
\[
  k=\lceil\log_2(\sqrt2\,\sigma\,T^2/C)\rceil,
\]
and let $W$ be the midpoint product with the equal-variation checkpoints of \Cref{lem:inverse-levels}, as in \Cref{lem:main}(2). Then $W$ has $(k+1)$-bit generators,
$n\le1+4\ell\,T^2/C$ unitary factors, and leakage
$\|(1-Q)WP\|\le2C/T$. For a target leakage $\delta>0$ and $T=2C/\delta$, provided
$\delta^2\le4\sqrt2\,\sigma C$, the entry precision and the number of unitaries obey
\begin{align}
  k+1&\le2\log_2(1/\delta)+\log_2(4\sqrt2\,\sigma C)+2,\nonumber\\
  n&\le1+16\ell C/\delta^2.\label{eq:target-cost}
\end{align}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We apply \Cref{lem:main}(2) at accuracy $\varepsilon=C/T$ to $H$, which has variation $\ell$
because the increasing rescaling $t\mapsto t/T$ preserves total variation.
Since $C/T>0$, for every $j\in\mathbb N$,
$2^j\ge\sqrt2\,\sigma\,T/(C/T)$ is equivalent to
$\log_2(\sqrt2\,\sigma\,T^2/C)\le j$.
Since $C\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,T^2$, the logarithm is nonnegative, so $k$ is the least
precision for accuracy $C/T$. \Cref{lem:main}(2) gives the count and $\|W-U(T)\|\le C/T$, so
$\|(1-Q)WP\|\le\|(1-Q)U(T)P\|+\|W-U(T)\|\le2C/T$.

For \eqref{eq:target-cost}, $\delta^2\le4\sqrt2\,\sigma C$ is
$C\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,T^2$ at $T=2C/\delta$. Substituting $T^2/C=4C/\delta^2$ in the count gives
$n\le1+4\ell T^2/C=1+16\ell C/\delta^2$, and in the precision gives
\begin{align*}
  k+1&\le\log_2(\sqrt2\,\sigma\,T^2/C)+2 &&\text{since $\lceil x\rceil\le x+1$}\\
  &=2\log_2(1/\delta)+\log_2(4\sqrt2\,\sigma C)+2 &&\text{since $T=2C/\delta$}.
\end{align*}

label: def:coordinates
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:coordinates}
The
\emph{coordinates} of a $d\times d$ Hermitian matrix are the real and imaginary parts of its entries on
and above the diagonal, $d^2$ of them once the vanishing imaginary parts on the diagonal
are dropped. A coordinate $h$ of $H$ is a real function
of $t$, and $2^k[h(t)]_k$ is its \emph{grid level}.
A family is \emph{piecewise monotone} if its coordinates are monotone on each interval of a finite partition.
head: environment

label: prop:pieces-exist
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:pieces-exist}
Let $k\ge0$ be an integer and $0=\xi_0<\xi_1<\dots<\xi_N=T$ be times such that every coordinate of $H$ is monotone
on each interval $[\xi_r,\xi_{r+1}]$. Then
$H^{(k)}$ is piecewise constant, with at most
\[
  \sum_{r=0}^{N-1}\Bigl(1+\sum_h\bigl\lceil 2^k\,
  |h(\xi_{r+1})-h(\xi_r)|\bigr\rceil\Bigr)
\]
pieces, the inner sum running over the coordinates of $H$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $[a,b]=[\xi_r,\xi_{r+1}]$. By Hermiticity, the grid levels
$v_h(t)=2^k[h(t)]_k$ determine $H^{(k)}(t)$.
Since truncation preserves monotonicity, each $v_h$ is monotone, so
$c(t)=\sum_h|v_h(t)-v_h(a)|$ is nondecreasing and increases whenever any $v_h$ changes.
Thus, $H^{(k)}$ is constant on each level set of $c$, an interval since $c$ is nondecreasing,
and $c$ takes values in $\{0,\ldots,c(b)\}$.
Discard singleton level sets, since values at piece endpoints do not matter (\Cref{sec:prelim}).
The remaining intervals are adjacent, since finitely many singletons cannot cover a positive-length gap,
and their interiors give the pieces, at most one per value of $c$.

Truncation satisfies $2^k([y]_k-[x]_k)\le\lceil2^k(y-x)\rceil$ whenever $x\le y$.
For $0\le x\le y$, this is the floor-difference inequality $\lfloor2^k y\rfloor-\lfloor2^k x\rfloor\le\lceil2^k(y-x)\rceil$.
For $x\le y\le0$, it follows from the nonnegative case for $-y\le-x$ by oddness,
and for opposite signs,
$2^k([y]_k-[x]_k)=\lfloor2^k y\rfloor+\lfloor2^k|x|\rfloor\le2^k(y-x)$.
Applying this to each monotone $h$ gives
\begin{align*}
  \#\{\text{pieces on }[a,b]\}&\le\#\{\text{values of }c\}\le1+c(b)\\
  &=1+\sum_h|v_h(b)-v_h(a)|\le1+\sum_h\bigl\lceil2^k|h(b)-h(a)|\bigr\rceil .
\end{align*}
Summing over the intervals gives the bound.

label: def:level-measure
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:level-measure}
A \emph{level measure} $\mu$ is the Stieltjes measure of a nondecreasing, right-continuous
function $F$, zero on $(-\infty,0]$ and taking finitely many values on every $[0,R]$.
Thus, $F(x)=\mu((0,x])$ for $x\ge0$.
Set
\[
  [x]_\mu=\int_{(0,\infty)}\mathbf1_{\{\lambda\le x\}}\,d\mu(\lambda)=F(x)
  \quad(x\ge0),\qquad [-x]_\mu=-[x]_\mu.
\]
Applying this entrywise to real and imaginary parts defines
$H^{(\mu)}$. The \emph{discrepancy} on $[0,R]$ is
$D_R(\mu)=\sup_{0\le x\le R}|x-F(x)|$.
The \emph{crossing number} $\operatorname{cr}_\mu(x,y)$ is one less than the number of distinct
values $[z]_\mu$ for $\min(x,y)\le z\le\max(x,y)$.
It counts the levels that a coordinate moving monotonically from $x$ to $y$ crosses, so it bounds how many times its truncation changes.
For a map $q$ on $[0,T]$, a \emph{layer} is a pre-image $q^{-1}(\{v\})$.
head: environment
name: Level measure

label: thm:general-levels
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:general-levels}
Let $\mu$ be a level measure, and let $H$ be a $\sigma$-sparse family whose coordinates (\Cref{def:coordinates}) have magnitude at most $R$ for every $t$.
Then $H^{(\mu)}$ is Hermitian, has a zero entry wherever $H$ does and hence is $\sigma$-sparse, and, for every $t$,
\[
  \|H(t)-H^{(\mu)}(t)\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,D_R(\mu).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The odd extension fixes zero, and oddness makes truncation of real and imaginary parts commute with complex conjugation, so
$H^{(\mu)}$ is Hermitian and preserves zeros. Since every coordinate lies in $[-R,R]$, the definition of $D_R(\mu)$ and oddness bound each coordinate
error by $D_R(\mu)$, hence each complex entry error by $\sqrt2\,D_R(\mu)$, and the row-sum bound of \Cref{lem:truncation-error} gives the result.
head: environment

label: thm:level-pieces
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:level-pieces}
Let $q$ be a map on $[0,T]$ taking finitely many values, with each layer $q^{-1}(\{v\})$ an interval.
Then $q$ is constant on each piece of a partition of $[0,T]$ into at most $|q([0,T])|$ pieces (\Cref{def:piecewise}).
Consequently, if the coordinates $h$ of $H$ (\Cref{def:coordinates}) are monotone on each interval $[\xi_r,\xi_{r+1}]$, where
$0=\xi_0<\dots<\xi_N=T$, then, for each level measure $\mu$ with crossing number $\operatorname{cr}_\mu$ (\Cref{def:level-measure}), $H^{(\mu)}$ is piecewise constant, with at most
\[
  \sum_{r=0}^{N-1}\Bigl(1+\sum_h\operatorname{cr}_\mu\bigl(h(\xi_r),h(\xi_{r+1})\bigr)\Bigr)
\]
pieces.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Cut $[0,T]$ at $0$ and each layer's supremum. These at most $1+|q([0,T])|$ cuts include $T$, the supremum of its layer, giving at most $|q([0,T])|$ open pieces. Finitely many layers cover each piece $(a,b)$, so one contains points arbitrarily close to $a$ and, being an interval, contains some $(a,c)$ with $c>a$. If it missed a point of $(a,b)$, its supremum would be a cut inside the piece, a contradiction.

For $t\in[\xi_r,\xi_{r+1}]$, monotonicity puts $h(t)$ between $h(\xi_r)$ and $h(\xi_{r+1})$, so $[h(t)]_\mu$ takes at most
$1+\operatorname{cr}_\mu(h(\xi_r),h(\xi_{r+1}))$ values.
Rank them from $0$ in the order in which $[h(t)]_\mu$ attains them. Since $[\cdot]_\mu$ is nondecreasing, $[h(t)]_\mu$ is monotone in $t$, so each rank is nondecreasing in $t$, the layers of the tuple of ranks are intervals, and the sum of the ranks increases whenever the tuple changes. Hence, the number of values of the tuple is at most the $r$th summand.
Equal ranks give equal truncated coordinates, and Hermiticity determines the lower-triangular entries, so the first claim, applied to the tuple, bounds the pieces of $H^{(\mu)}$ on $[\xi_r,\xi_{r+1}]$ by that summand. Summing over $r$ gives the bound.
head: environment

label: cor:level-main
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:level-main}
Let $H$ be $\sigma$-sparse on $[0,T]$, with coordinates of magnitude at most $R$.
Let $0<\varepsilon\le\sqrt2\,\sigma T$, let $k$ be the least nonnegative integer
with $2^k\ge\sqrt2\,\sigma T/\varepsilon$, and let $\mu$ be a level measure with
discrepancy $D_R(\mu)\le2^{-k-1}$.
For checkpoints $0=t_0\le\cdots\le t_n=T$, let $A_j=H((t_j+t_{j+1})/2)$ and define
\[
  W_\mu=e^{-i(t_n-t_{n-1})A_{n-1}^{(\mu)}}\cdots e^{-i(t_1-t_0)A_0^{(\mu)}}.
\]
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $H$ is regulated, some checkpoints give
$\|W_\mu-U(T)\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma2^{-k}T\le\varepsilon$.
\item For $H$ of total variation $0<\ell<\infty$, equal-variation checkpoints (\Cref{lem:inverse-levels})
give this bound with
$n=\lceil2^{k+1}\ell/(\sqrt2\,\sigma)\rceil\le1+4T\ell/\varepsilon$.
\item If $H$ is $L$-Lipschitz with $L>0$, uniform checkpoints $t_j=jT/n$
give the same bound with
$n=\lceil2^{k+1}L T/(\sqrt2\,\sigma)\rceil\le1+4L T^2/\varepsilon$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The checkpoints and counts in \Cref{lem:main} are independent of $\mu$.
For $t_j<t<t_{j+1}$, the oscillation bound in its proof gives $\|H(t)-A_j\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k-1}$, and
\Cref{thm:general-levels} gives $\|A_j-A_j^{(\mu)}\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,D_R(\mu)\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k-1}$. Thus, $\|H(t)-A_j^{(\mu)}\|\le\sqrt2\,\sigma\,2^{-k}$,
and since the generators $A_j^{(\mu)}$ are Hermitian, \Cref{lem:duhamel} and the choice of $k$ give the claimed error.

label: thm:level-evolution
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Gluing constant evolutions gives the product, and by definition,
$M_{n-1}=U^\dagger V-iU^\dagger Y_{n-1}V$ and $M_{-1}(a_0)=1$.
Telescoping the corrected comparisons, with $Y_{-1}=0$, gives
\begin{align*}
 U(T)^\dagger V(T)-1
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\Bigl[\bigl(U^\dagger(1-iY_j)V\bigr)(a_{j+1})
                       -\bigl(U^\dagger(1-iY_j)V\bigr)(a_j)\Bigr]\\
 &\quad-i\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\bigl(U^\dagger(Y_j-Y_{j-1})V\bigr)(a_j)
       +i\bigl(U^\dagger Y_{n-1}V\bigr)(T).
\end{align*}
Unitary invariance, $\|V(T)-U(T)\|=\|U(T)^\dagger V(T)-1\|$, and the triangle inequality give \eqref{eq:layer-assembly}.

label: lem:cell
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cell}
Let $h$ be Hermitian, with the frame operator $\Theta_h$ defined and $\|\Theta_h\|\le N$, let $D$ be any matrix, and let $K$ be a continuous Hamiltonian on $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$.
Put $\bar Y=\Theta_h(D)$, $\Delta(\tau)=K(\tau)-h$, and $\omega(\tau)=N+\tfrac18-\tau^2/2$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The solution of $\dot Y+i[h,Y]=\tau D$, $Y(-\tfrac12)=\bar Y$, satisfies
$Y(\tfrac12)=\bar Y$.
\item For unitary evolutions $i\dot U=KU$, $i\dot V=hV$, the comparison $M=U^\dagger(1-iY)V$ satisfies
\[
 \|M(\tfrac12)-M(-\tfrac12)\|
 \le\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\bigl[\|\Delta(\tau)-\tau D\|+
          \omega(\tau)\|\Delta(\tau)\|\,\|D\|\bigr]\,d\tau .
\]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Substituting $\sigma=\tau+\tfrac12$ in \eqref{eq:frame} gives
\[
 e^{ih}\bar Ye^{-ih}-\bar Y
 =\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\tau e^{i(\tau+1/2)h}De^{-i(\tau+1/2)h}\,d\tau=R.
\]
Write $E(s)=s\,e^{i(s+1/2)h}De^{-i(s+1/2)h}$, so that $\|E(s)\|=|s|\,\|D\|$. Then
\begin{align*}
 Y(\tau)&=e^{-i(\tau+1/2)h}\Bigl[\bar Y+\int_{-1/2}^{\tau}E(s)\,ds\Bigr]e^{i(\tau+1/2)h} &&\text{variation of constants},\\
 &=e^{-i(\tau-1/2)h}\Bigl[\bar Y-\int_{\tau}^{1/2}e^{-ih}E(s)e^{ih}\,ds\Bigr]e^{i(\tau-1/2)h} &&\text{by the Stein equation},\\
 \|Y(\tau)\|&\le\Bigl(N+\int_{|\tau|}^{1/2}s\,ds\Bigr)\|D\|=\omega(\tau)\|D\| &&\text{first line if }\tau\le0,\text{ second if }\tau\ge0,
\end{align*}
by unitary invariance and $\|\bar Y\|\le N\|D\|$,
and the second line at $\tau=\tfrac12$ gives $Y(\tfrac12)=\bar Y$.
The product rule and the equation for $Y$ give
$\dot M=U^\dagger[i(\Delta-\tau D)+\Delta Y]V$,
so integration and $\|\Delta Y\|\le\|\Delta\|\|Y\|$ give (2).

label: def:unit-coefficients
title: Definition
head: environment

label: thm:unit-steps
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:unit-steps}
Let $T$, $H$, $U$, and $W_T$ be as in \Cref{def:unit-product}.
Suppose that $H$ is differentiable, $\|H'\|\leL$,
$\|H'(s)-H'(s')\|\le2\nu|s-s'|$, and each sample $H(j/T)$, $0<j<T$, is $\gamma$-separated of width at most $\barw$ (\Cref{def:exponential-operators}). Then
\[
 \bigl\|W_T-e^{iH(1)/2}U(T)e^{-iH(0)/2}\bigr\|
 \le\frac{c_0L+c_1L^2+c_2\nu}{T},
\]
with $c_i$ from \Cref{def:unit-coefficients}, or $c_i(w)$ for width at most $w<2\pi$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For each full piece, set $h_j=H(j/T)$, $D_j=H'(j/T)/T$,
$\Delta_j(\tau)=H((j+\tau)/T)-h_j$, and $Y_j=\Theta_{h_j}(D_j)$,
and let $R_j$ be the integral in \Cref{lem:cell}(2) with $N_\gamma$ for $N$.
By \Cref{lem:cell}(1), the varying correction equals $Y_j$ at both endpoints, so $R_j$ bounds the increment with constant $Y_j$ in \eqref{eq:layer-assembly}.
With $Y_{-1}=Y_0=Y_T=0$ and $M_j=U^\dagger(1-iY_j)V$ as in \Cref{thm:level-evolution}, \Cref{lem:duhamel} bounds the two half-piece increments by $B_T$. In \eqref{eq:layer-assembly} over $T+1$ pieces, the last jump is $\|Y_{T-1}\|$ and the final correction vanishes, giving, by \eqref{eq:rounded}, the error bound
\begin{align*}
 B_T&=\int_0^{1/2}\|H(t/T)-H(0)\|\,dt
       +\int_{T-1/2}^{T}\|H(t/T)-H(1)\|\,dt,\\
 E_T&=B_T+\sum_{j=1}^{T-1}(R_j+\|Y_j-Y_{j-1}\|)+\|Y_{T-1}\|.
\end{align*}
Since $\Delta_j(\tau)-\tau D_j=\int_0^\tau\bigl(H'((j+s)/T)-H'(j/T)\bigr)\,ds/T$, integrating the derivative bounds gives
$\|\Delta_j\|\leL|\tau|/T$, $\|D_j\|\leL/T$, and
$\|\Delta_j-\tau D_j\|\le\nu\tau^2/T^2$, so $B_T\leL/(4T)$ and
\[
 R_j\le\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\Bigl[\frac{\nu\tau^2}{T^2}+\omega(\tau)\frac{L^2|\tau|}{T^2}\Bigr]d\tau
 =\frac{\nu/12+(N_\gamma/4+1/64)L^2}{T^2},
\]
by $\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\tau^2\,d\tau=1/12$ and $\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}|\tau|\omega(\tau)\,d\tau=N_\gamma/4+1/64$.
The derivative hypotheses give $\|D_j-D_{j-1}\|\le2\nu/T^2$ and $\|h_j-h_{j-1}\|\leL/T$. Hence, \Cref{lem:bernoulli-inverse} bounds the end frames by $N_\gammaL/T$ and each internal jump by
$N_\gamma\|D_j-D_{j-1}\|+N'_\gamma\|h_j-h_{j-1}\|\|D_{j-1}\|\le(2N_\gamma\nu+N'_\gammaL^2)/T^2$.
For $T\ge2$, adding $B_T$, the $T-1$ pieces, the two end frames, and the $T-2$ internal jumps gives
\begin{align*}
 E_T&\le\frac{L}{4T}+(T-1)\frac{\nu/12+(N_\gamma/4+1/64)L^2}{T^2}
 +\frac{2N_\gammaL}{T}+(T-2)\frac{2N_\gamma\nu+N'_\gammaL^2}{T^2}\\
 &\le\frac{c_0L+c_1L^2+c_2\nu}{T} &&\text{by \eqref{eq:unit-coefficients}}.
\end{align*}
For $T=1$, $E_T=B_T\leL/4$,
and the width specialization follows from \Cref{lem:bernoulli-inverse}(2).

label: thm:unit-steps-dat
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:unit-steps-dat}
With the hypotheses and constants of \Cref{thm:unit-steps}, let $P,Q$ be orthogonal projectors commuting with $H(0),H(1)$, respectively, for example their spectral projectors. Then
\[
  \Bigl|\,\|(1-Q)W_TP\|-\|(1-Q)U(T)P\|\,\Bigr|\le\frac{c_0L+c_1L^2+c_2\nu}{T}.
\]
In particular, if a continuous adiabatic theorem bounds by $\varepsilon$ the leakage
$\|(1-Q)U(T)P\|$ of $H$ over the time $T$, then
$\|(1-Q)W_TP\|\le\varepsilon+(c_0L+c_1L^2+c_2\nu)/T$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The endpoint commutations and unitary invariance give
\[
 \|(1-Q)e^{iH(1)/2}U(T)e^{-iH(0)/2}P\|=\|(1-Q)U(T)P\|.
\]
Since $\|1-Q\|,\|P\|\le1$, compression preserves the bound from \Cref{thm:unit-steps},
and the reverse triangle inequality gives the claim.

label: prop:balanced-pieces
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:balanced-pieces}
Let $a_0<\cdots<a_n$, and let $K$ be a continuous Hamiltonian on $[a_0,a_n]$, with evolution $U$, $U(a_0)=1$. Sample each $[a_j,a_{j+1}]$ at its midpoint $\xi_j$.
Put $\lambda_j=a_{j+1}-a_j$, and suppose $h_j=\lambda_jK(\xi_j)$ is $\gamma$-separated of width at most $\barw$.
For Hermitian slopes $D_j$, set $Y_j=\Theta_{h_j}(D_j)$, $Y_{-1}=0$, and let $R_j$ be the integral in \Cref{lem:cell}(2) with $N_\gamma$ for $N$ and $\Delta_j(\tau)=\lambda_jK(\xi_j+\lambda_j\tau)-h_j$. Then
\[
 \|e^{-ih_{n-1}}\cdots e^{-ih_0}-U(a_n)\|
 \le\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(R_j+\|Y_j-Y_{j-1}\|)+\|Y_{n-1}\|.
\]
For width at most $w<2\pi$, use $\mathcal N(w)$ in $R_j$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
On piece $j$, the chain rule with $t=\xi_j+\lambda_j\tau$ gives the rescaled generator $\lambda_jK(\xi_j+\lambda_j\tau)$ and constant generator $h_j$.
With slope $D_j$ and bound $N_\gamma$, or $\mathcal N(w)$ under the width bound, the endpoint equality of \Cref{lem:cell} gives the increment bound $R_j$ for $M_j=U^\dagger(1-iY_j)V$, where $V$ is the piecewise-constant evolution.
Translating $a_0$ to zero, \Cref{thm:level-evolution} identifies the evolution generated by $K(\xi_j)$ on each $(a_j,a_{j+1})$ with the displayed product, and its assembly bound \eqref{eq:layer-assembly} gives the claim.

label: cor:unit-steps-jrs
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:unit-steps-jrs}
Assume the continuous Jansen--Ruskai--Seiler theorem \cite[Theorem~3]{jansen2007}.
Fix an integer $T\ge1$. Let $H$ be $C^2$ on an open interval containing $[0,1]$, with $\|H'\|\leL$ and $\|H''\|\le2\nu$, and let $H(j/T)$ be $\gamma$-separated of width at most $\barw$ for $0<j<T$. Let $I$ be a compact interval. Suppose that, for $0\le s\le1$,
exactly $m$ eigenvalues of $H(s)$, counted with multiplicity, lie in $I$, and the others
are at distance at least $g(s)>0$ from $I$, with $g$ continuous. Let $P,Q$ be the spectral
projectors of $H(0),H(1)$ for $I$. Then the product $W_T$ of \eqref{eq:unit-product} satisfies
\[
  \|(1-Q)W_TP\|
  \le\frac{J_m(\|H'\|,\|H''\|,g)+c_0L+c_1L^2+c_2\nu}{T},
\]
with the Jansen--Ruskai--Seiler coefficient $J_m$ of \Cref{def:jrs-coefficient} and $c_i$ from \Cref{def:unit-coefficients}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Jansen--Ruskai--Seiler \cite[Theorem~3]{jansen2007} bounds $\|(1-Q)U(T)P\|$ by
$J_m(\|H'\|,\|H''\|,g)/T$. Integrating $\|H''\|\le2\nu$ gives the Lipschitz bound on $H'$ required by \Cref{thm:unit-steps-dat}, which adds $(c_0L+c_1L^2+c_2\nu)/T$.

label: def:aqc-schedule
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:aqc-schedule}
For $\kappa\ge1$ and $p>0$, An and Lin's AQC($p$) schedule \cite[Eq.~(5)]{anlin2022} is the solution $f$ of
\[
 f'=a_p(1-f+f/\kappa)^p,\qquad f(0)=0,\qquad
 a_p=\int_0^1(1-u+u/\kappa)^{-p}\,du.
\]
Here $1-f+f/\kappa$ is the gap lower bound in \Cref{cor:qlsp-unit-steps}. The normalization gives $f(1)=1$. For $p=3/2$ and $\kappa>1$, separating variables gives
\[
 f(s)=\frac{1-(1+rs)^{-2}}{1-(1+r)^{-2}},\qquad r=\sqrt\kappa-1,
\]
while $f(s)=s$ for $\kappa=1$.
head: environment

label: cor:qlsp-unit-steps
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:qlsp-unit-steps}
Assume the continuous multiplicity-one Jansen--Ruskai--Seiler theorem \cite[Theorem~3]{jansen2007}.
Let $A$ be Hermitian positive definite with $\|A\|=1$ and condition number
$\kappa\ge1$, and let $\|b\|=1$. With $Q_b=1-|b\rangle\langle b|$, let $H=(1-f)H_0+fH_1$ be
the An--Lin path with the AQC($3/2$) schedule of \Cref{def:aqc-schedule} and $P(s)$ the projector onto $([(1-f(s))+f(s)A]^{-1}b,0)$, where
\[
 H_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&Q_b\\Q_b&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 H_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&AQ_b\\Q_bA&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Assume An and Lin's gap bound \cite[Appendix~A]{anlin2022}: the nonzero eigenvalues of $H(s)$ are at
distance at least $g(s)=1-f(s)+f(s)/\kappa$ from $0$. If $\kappa>1$, then, for
every integer $T\ge1$, the product \eqref{eq:unit-product} satisfies
\[
 \|(1-P(1))W_TP(0)\|\le\frac{5\,J_1(|f'|,|f''|,g)}{4T}\le\frac{45\kappa}{T},
\]
with the Jansen--Ruskai--Seiler coefficient $J_1$ of \Cref{def:jrs-coefficient}. If $\kappa=1$, then $(1-P(1))W_TP(0)=0$. Thus, for $\delta>0$,
$\lceil45\kappa/\delta\rceil$ unit steps give leakage at most $\delta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The block norm bound
$\left\|\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&B\\B^\dagger&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\right\|\le\|B\|$
and $\|Q_b\|,\|A\|,\|1-A\|\le1$ give $\|H_0\|,\|H_1\|,\|H_1-H_0\|\le1$.
Since $0\le f\le1$, convexity gives $\|H\|\le1$, hence width at most $2$.
In block form, $H$ has off-diagonal blocks $[(1-f)+fA]Q_b$ and its adjoint, with $(1-f)+fA$ positive, so the range of $P(s)$ and $(0,b)$ span the kernel of $H(s)$, and $H P=PH=0$.
If $\kappa=1$, positivity and $\|A\|=\|A^{-1}\|=1$ give $A=1$, so the path is constant
and every step acts as the identity on its kernel.

Assume $\kappa>1$, and put $J=J_1(|f'|,|f''|,g)$ and $S=|(0,b)\rangle\langle(0,b)|$. Since $H S=SH=0$ and $SP(s)=0$, the operator
$H+S$ has derivatives $f'(H_1-H_0)$ and $f''(H_1-H_0)$, of norms at most $|f'|$ and $|f''|$, the simple eigenvalue $0$ with projector $P(s)$, and gap at least $g$, since $S$ moves $(0,b)$ to eigenvalue $1\ge g$.
Its evolution $U(t)e^{-itS}$ agrees with $U(t)$ on $\operatorname{ran}P(0)$,
so Jansen--Ruskai--Seiler, whose coefficient increases with the derivative norms, gives leakage at most $J/T$.

With $L=2(1+r)^2/(r+2)$, differentiation, $1-(1+r)^{-2}=r(r+2)/(1+r)^2$, and
$\kappa=(1+r)^2$ give $g=(1+rs)^{-2}$, $f'=L(1+rs)^{-3}$, and $f''=-3rL(1+rs)^{-4}$,
hence the bounds
$\|H'\|\leL$ and $\|H''\|\le3rL$.
The width-$2$ specialization in \Cref{thm:unit-steps}, with $c_i=c_i(2)$ and $\nu=\tfrac32rL$, gives
comparison error at most $E=(c_0L+c_1L^2+\tfrac32c_2rL)/T$. By \Cref{thm:unit-steps-dat}, leakage is at most $J/T+E$.
Evaluating \eqref{eq:jrs-coefficient} at $m=1$, the endpoint terms $f'(0)/g(0)^2=L$ and $f'(1)/g(1)^2=L(1+r)$ and constant integrands $|f''|/g^2=3rL$ and $7f'^2/g^3=7L^2$ give
\[
 J=L+L(1+r)+3rL+7L^2=(4r+2)L+7L^2\le36\kappa,
\]
using $L\le2(1+r)$ and $4r+2\le4(1+r)$.

Since $\pi>3$, the bounds \eqref{eq:frame-majorants} give $\mathcal N(2)\le1/8$ and $\mathcal N'(2)\le1/64$,
so \eqref{eq:unit-coefficients} gives $c_0,c_2\le1/2$ and $c_1\le1/64+1/32+1/32=5/64$.
Since $r,L>0$, these bounds give $TE\le J/4$ term by term:
\[
 c_0L\le\frac{L+L(1+r)}4,\qquad
 c_1L^2\le\frac{5L^2}{64}\le\frac{7L^2}4,\qquad
 c_2\frac{3rL}2\le\frac{3rL}4.
\]
Adding gives leakage at most $5J/(4T)\le45\kappa/T\le\delta$ when $T\ge45\kappa/\delta$.

label: def:walk
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:walk}
A \emph{walk} is an ordered sequence of unitaries.
The walk is \emph{compatible} with a differentiable unitary-valued family $W$ on $[0,1]$
when its $T$ steps are $W(j/T)$, with product
\[
  W_T=W((T-1)/T)\cdotsW(0).
\]
head: environment

label: thm:unit-steps-walk
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:unit-steps-walk}
Let $T\ge1$ be an integer, let $w<2\pi$, and let $W$ be differentiable and unitary on $[0,1]$, with
$\|W'\|\leL$ and $\|W'(s)-W'(s')\|\le2\nu|s-s'|$.
Suppose that some open arc of length $2\pi-w$ meets the spectrum of no $W(s)$.
Then there is a differentiable Hermitian path $\Lambda$ on $[0,1]$ with $e^{-i\Lambda}=W$ such that, for the product $W_T$ of the compatible walk and evolution $U_\Lambda$ of $\Lambda(t/T)$,
\[
 \bigl\|W_T-e^{i\Lambda(1)/2}U_\Lambda(T)e^{-i\Lambda(0)/2}\bigr\|
 \le\frac{c_0L_\Lambda+c_1L_\Lambda^2+c_2\nu_\Lambda}{T},
\]
where $c_i=c_i(w)$, $L_\Lambda=\mathcal BL$, and $\nu_\Lambda=\mathcal B(\nu+(\tfrac12+\mathcal B')L^2)$, with the Bernoulli majorant $\mathcal B$ of \Cref{def:exponential-operators} and its derivative $\mathcal B'$ evaluated at $w$.
The path has spectral width at most $w$, is $C^2$ wherever $W$ is $C^2$, and satisfies
\[
 \|\Lambda'\|\leL_\Lambda,\qquad
 \|\Lambda'(s)-\Lambda'(s')\|\le2\nu_\Lambda|s-s'|.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write the complementary closed arc as $\{e^{-i\theta}:\theta\in I\}$, with $I$ a closed interval of length $w$.
Diagonalizing $W(s)=\sum_k e^{-i\theta_k}P_k$ with $\theta_k\in I$, we set $\Lambda(s)=\sum_k\theta_kP_k$, which is Hermitian with $e^{-i\Lambda(s)}=W(s)$ and spectral width at most $w$.
Hermitian matrices with spectrum in the compact interval $I$ form a compact set. If $s_n\to s$, any subsequential limit is Hermitian, has spectrum in $I$, and exponentiates to $W(s)$ by continuity of the exponential. Injectivity of $\theta\mapsto e^{-i\theta}$ on $I$ makes this limit uniquely $\Lambda(s)$, proving continuity. The exponential has invertible differential by
\Cref{lem:bernoulli-inverse}, so its smooth local inverse preserves differentiability and $C^2$ regularity. Differentiating $W=e^{-i\Lambda}$ by \eqref{eq:exp-derivative} gives $W'=-iW\,\Phi_\Lambda(\Lambda')$, so
$\Lambda'=\Phi_\Lambda^{-1}(iW^{\dagger}W')$.
Unitarity and \Cref{lem:bernoulli-inverse} give
$\|\Lambda'\|\le\mathcal BL$, so $\|\Lambda(s)-\Lambda(s')\|\le\mathcal BL|s-s'|$. Adding and subtracting $W(s)^\daggerW'(s')$ gives
\begin{align*}
  \Lambda'(s)-\Lambda'(s')
  &=\Phi_{\Lambda(s)}^{-1}\bigl(iW(s)^\dagger(W'(s)-W'(s'))+i(W(s)-W(s'))^\daggerW'(s')\bigr)\\
  &\quad+\bigl(\Phi_{\Lambda(s)}^{-1}-\Phi_{\Lambda(s')}^{-1}\bigr)\bigl(iW(s')^\daggerW'(s')\bigr),
\end{align*}
which implies, by \Cref{lem:bernoulli-inverse}, the bounds on $W'$ and $\Lambda$, and
$\|W(s)-W(s')\|\leL|s-s'|$ obtained by integrating $\|W'\|\leL$, that
\[
  \|\Lambda'(s)-\Lambda'(s')\|
  \le\mathcal B\,(2\nu+L^2)|s-s'|+2\mathcal B'\cdot\mathcal BL|s-s'|\cdotL
  =2\mathcal B\,(\nu+(\tfrac12+\mathcal B')L^2)|s-s'| .
\]
Since $e^{-i\Lambda(j/T)}=W(j/T)$, \Cref{thm:unit-steps} for $\Lambda$ gives the comparison.

label: def:qlsp-walk-construction
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:qlsp-walk-construction}
Put $\alpha(f)=\sqrt{(1-f)^2+f^2}$.
Use four qubits, ordered as in $L$, followed by the space $\operatorname{codom}V$ of $O$.
Put $Q_0=\operatorname{diag}(VQ_bV^\dagger,0)$,
\[
 R_{1,0}=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\0&-I\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 R_{0,1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\I&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 R=\frac{(1-f)R_{1,0}+fR_{0,1}}{\alpha},
\]
\[
 \Pi=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}I&I\\I&-I\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \Pi_Q=\begin{pmatrix}Q_0&I-Q_0\\I-Q_0&Q_0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \Pi_1=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&\sqrt3/2\\\sqrt3/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix},
\]
and $G=\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{diag}(R,R),\Pi_Q\operatorname{diag}(\Pi,\Pi))$.
The outer block indices of $G$, of $\Pi_Q$, and of $R$ and $\Pi$ correspond to qubits 2, 3, and 4,
respectively. The operator $\operatorname{diag}(I,O,I,O)$ applies $O$ when qubit 4 is $|1\rangle$.
Define
\[
 E=\Pi_1\otimes
 \left[G\left(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\otimes
 \operatorname{diag}(I,O,I,O)\right)G^\dagger\right].
\]
Put $Z=I_2\otimes\operatorname{diag}(I,0,Q_0,I-Q_0)$ to isolate the solution line.
Fix $\kappa>1$ with AQC($3/2$) schedule $f$ (\Cref{def:aqc-schedule}). Define
$W(s)=(2LL^\dagger-I)E(f(s))$ and $F_s=(I+iE(f(s)))/\sqrt2$.

label: cor:qlsp-walk
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:qlsp-walk}
Let $O$ be a Hermitian involution, $V$ an isometry, $A=V^\dagger OV$ positive definite,
and $\|b\|=1$. Assume, for some $\kappa>1$, that every nonzero eigenvalue of $H(f)$ has absolute value at least $1-f+f/\kappa$ for $0\le f\le1$ \cite[Appendix~A]{anlin2022}. Assume also the
continuous multiplicity-one Jansen--Ruskai--Seiler theorem \cite[Theorem~3]{jansen2007}. Use AQC($3/2$) with
\[
 r=\sqrt\kappa-1,\qquad
 f(s)=\frac{1-(1+rs)^{-2}}{1-(1+r)^{-2}}.
\]
The walk $W(s)$ of \Cref{def:qlsp-walk-construction} uses one controlled $O$ query per step.
For the constant $K>0$ of \Cref{lem:qlsp-walk-constants}:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every integer $T\ge1$,
\[
 \|(I-P(1))W((T-1)/T)\cdots W(0)P(0)\|\le\frac{K\kappa}{T},
\]
where $P(s)$ projects onto the line through $F_sL([(1-f(s))I+f(s)A]^{-1}b,0)$, a $+i$
eigenvector of $W(s)$.
Thus, for $0<\delta\le1$,
$\lceil K\kappa/\delta\rceil$ steps suffice for leakage at most $\delta$.
\item For $0<\delta\le1$, put $N=\lceil2K\kappa/\delta\rceil$.
Starting from $L(b,0)$, apply controlled $E(f(0))$ with its control prepared in $(|0\rangle+i|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and measured, succeeding on outcome $(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$, take $N$ walk steps, and apply controlled $E(f(1))$ in the same way with the control prepared in $(|0\rangle-i|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
The walk leakage is at most $\delta/2$.
Each endpoint succeeds with probability $1/2$, so joint success has probability $1/4$. Conditioned on success, the normalized output is within distance $\delta$, up to a global
phase, of $L(A^{-1}b/\|A^{-1}b\|,0)$.
Each attempt uses $N+2\le(2K+3)\kappa/\delta$ controlled $O$ queries, excluding preparing $b$, implementing $Q_b$, and operations built from $V$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \Cref{lem:qlsp-walk-circuit}, $E$ is a Hermitian involution with the compression stated before \Cref{cor:qlsp-walk}.

For real $f$, $\|A\|=\|V^\dagger OV\|\le1$ gives $\|H_0\|,\|H_1\|\le1$ and hence $\|H(f)\|\le|1-f|+|f|\le\sqrt2\,\alpha$ by Cauchy--Schwarz, so the compression norm is at most $1/2$. For a compression eigenpair $(\lambda,v)$, $WLv=2\lambda Lv-ELv$ and $WELv=Lv$ give the walk phases
$\exp(\pm i\arccos\lambda)$, $\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(L^\dagger EL)$.
On the complement of these invariant planes, $W$ acts as $-E$, with eigenvalues $\pm1$. Since $\arccos\lambda\in[\pi/3,2\pi/3]$, cutting $i\log$ inside the free phase arc $(0,\pi/3)$ gives, by the local inverse argument of \Cref{thm:unit-steps-walk}, a $C^2$ Hermitian logarithm where $1+rs>0$, with spectrum in
$[-2\pi,-\pi/3]$.
The cut sends $+i$ to the
logarithm eigenvalue $-\pi/2$, and the gap bound $1-f+f/\kappa=(1+rs)^{-2}$, by the formula for $f$, gives it gap at least $1/[2\sqrt2\,\alpha(1+rs)^2]$ on $[0,1]$.
Indeed, compression scales the gap of $H(f)$ by $1/(2\sqrt2\,\alpha)$, the phases $e^{i\arccos\lambda}$ have logarithm eigenvalues $-\arccos\lambda$ with $|\arccos\lambda-\pi/2|=|\arcsin\lambda|\ge|\lambda|$, and the logarithm eigenvalues of $e^{-i\arccos\lambda}$ and $\pm1$ lie at least $\pi/2$ from $-\pi/2$.

Write $\Lambda$ for the full logarithm, with majorants evaluated at $w=5\pi/3$, and recall from \Cref{def:exponential-operators} that
$a_\Lambda(X)=i(\Lambda X-X\Lambda)$ and
$\Phi_\Lambda=\int_0^1 e^{\tau a_\Lambda}\,d\tau$, and from \Cref{lem:bernoulli-inverse}(3) that
$\Phi_\Lambda^{-1}=\sum_{n\ge0}(B_n/n!)a_\Lambda^n$.
Splitting this integral at $1/2$ gives
$\Phi_\Lambda=\tfrac12(1+e^{a_\Lambda/2})\Phi_{\Lambda/2}$.
Since these functions of $a_\Lambda$ commute, $2\Phi_{\Lambda/2}^{-1}=(1+e^{a_\Lambda/2})\Phi_\Lambda^{-1}$, which rearranges to the first identity below.
Unitary conjugation $e^{-a_\Lambda/2}$ preserves the norm, and the Bernoulli-series factors
$2-2^n$ are $1,0$ at $n=0,1$ and negative for $n\ge2$. Hence, using
the closed form $\mathcal B(x)=2+x/2-(x/2)\cot(x/2)$ (derived in the proof of
\Cref{lem:qlsp-walk-constants}) and $\cot(y/2)-\cot y=1/\sin y$,
\begin{align*}
  \Phi_\Lambda^{-1}
  &=\bigl(2\Phi_{\Lambda/2}^{-1}-\Phi_\Lambda^{-1}\bigr)e^{-a_\Lambda/2},\\
  2\Phi_{\Lambda/2}^{-1}-\Phi_\Lambda^{-1}
  &=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(2-2^n)B_n}{n!}(a_\Lambda/2)^n,\\
  \|\Phi_\Lambda^{-1}\|
  &\le\mathcal B(w)-2\mathcal B(w/2)+2\\
  &=\frac w2\left(\cot\frac w4-\cot\frac w2\right)
   =\frac{w/2}{\sin(w/2)}.
\end{align*}
Since $\sin(w/2)=1/2$, the bound is $5\pi/3$, sharper than the bound $\mathcal B(5\pi/3)>9$ of \Cref{lem:bernoulli-inverse}. The identity $\Lambda'=\Phi_\Lambda^{-1}(iW^\dagger W')$ (proof of \Cref{thm:unit-steps-walk}) and its derivative, with $\|(\Phi_\Lambda^{-1})'\|\le2\mathcal B'\|\Lambda'\|$ (\Cref{lem:bernoulli-inverse}) and $\|(iW^\dagger W')'\|\le\|W''\|+\|W'\|^2$, give
\[
 \|\Lambda'\|\le\tfrac{5\pi}3\|W'\|,\qquad
 \|\Lambda''\|\le\tfrac{5\pi}3\|W''\|+\tfrac{5\pi}3(1+2\mathcal B')\|W'\|^2.
\]
The fixed orthogonal projector $Z$ commutes with $E$ and every step, hence with $F_s$ and the logarithm, and satisfies
$ZL=L\operatorname{diag}(I,Q_b)$ (\Cref{lem:qlsp-walk-circuit}).
The invariant planes give the phase $\pi/2$ only at $\lambda=0$, so the $+i$ eigenspace of $W(s)$ is $F_sL\ker H(f(s))$, and $ZF_sL=F_sL\operatorname{diag}(I,Q_b)$. Since
$\ker H(f)=\{(z[(1-f)I+fA]^{-1}b,z'b):z,z'\in\mathbb C\}$ meets
$\operatorname{ran}\operatorname{diag}(I,Q_b)$ in the line through
$([(1-f)I+fA]^{-1}b,0)$, the $+i$ eigenspace of $W(s)$ on $\operatorname{ran}Z$ is $\operatorname{ran}P(s)$.

Define $\widehat\Lambda=Z\Lambda Z-(7\pi/6)(I-Z)$. It agrees with $\Lambda$ on the invariant subspace
$\operatorname{ran}Z$, so $e^{-i\widehat\Lambda(s)}Z=W(s)Z$, and equals $-7\pi/6$, the midpoint of $[-2\pi,-\pi/3]$, on its orthogonal complement,
so its spectrum stays in that interval and its $-\pi/2$ band is $\operatorname{ran}P(s)$.
The added eigenvalue is $2\pi/3$ from the band, preserving the gap bound
$1/[2\sqrt2\,\alpha(1+rs)^2]\le1/2$, since $\alpha\ge1/\sqrt2$ and $s\ge0$.
Since $Z$ is fixed, $\widehat\Lambda'=Z\Lambda'Z$ and $\widehat\Lambda''=Z\Lambda''Z$,
so projector contraction preserves both derivative bounds.
Since $W(s)$ and $e^{-i\widehat\Lambda(s)}$ commute with $Z$ and agree on $\operatorname{ran}Z$, and $ZP(0)=P(0)$, their products agree on $\operatorname{ran}P(0)$.
Thus, substituting \Cref{lem:qlsp-walk-circuit}(2) into the derivative bounds lets us apply
\Cref{lem:qlsp-walk-constants} to $\widehat\Lambda$.
With $J_1$, $g$, $\rho_1$, $\rho_2$, and $c_i$ from \Cref{lem:qlsp-walk-constants}, every integer $T\ge1$ satisfies
\begin{align*}
 \|(I-P(1))W((T-1)/T)\cdots W(0)P(0)\|
 &\le\frac{J_1+(4c_0\rho_1+16c_1\rho_1^2+6c_2\rho_2)(1+r)^2}T\\
 &\le\frac{K(1+r)^2}T=\frac{K\kappa}T.
\end{align*}
The first uses Jansen--Ruskai--Seiler, monotonicity in derivative norms, and \Cref{thm:unit-steps-dat} with \Cref{lem:qlsp-walk-constants}(3). Part~(2) and $K$'s definition give the second, and $1+r=\sqrt\kappa$ gives equality. Taking $T=\lceil K\kappa/\delta\rceil$ or $\lceil2K\kappa/\delta\rceil$ bounds leakage by $\delta$ or $\delta/2$, respectively.
 

Finally, control preparation and postselection give
$(I+iE(f(0)))/2=F_0/\sqrt2$ and $(I-iE(f(1)))/2=F_1^\dagger/\sqrt2$.
Since $F_s$ is unitary, each succeeds with probability $1/2$, hence $1/4$ jointly.
By the definition of $P(s)$, $f(0)=0$, and $f(1)=1$, $F_0L(b,0)$ spans $\operatorname{ran}P(0)$ and, with $x=A^{-1}b/\|A^{-1}b\|$, $F_1L(x,0)$ spans $\operatorname{ran}P(1)$. Let $\psi$ be the walk product applied to $F_0L(b,0)$, so the normalized successful joint output is $F_1^\dagger\psi$, and put $\chi=F_1^\dagger P(1)\psi$.
Since $F_1$ is unitary and $\delta\le1$, the leakage bound $\delta/2$ of $\lceil2K\kappa/\delta\rceil$ steps gives
$\|F_1^\dagger\psi-\chi\|=\|(I-P(1))\psi\|\le\delta/2<1$.
The reverse triangle inequality gives $\chi\ne0$ and
$|1-\|\chi\||\le\|F_1^\dagger\psi-\chi\|$, so homogeneity and the triangle inequality give
\[
 \left\|F_1^\dagger\psi-\frac\chi{\|\chi\|}\right\|
 \le\|F_1^\dagger\psi-\chi\|+|1-\|\chi\||\le\delta.
\]
Since $P(1)\psi$ lies in the line through $F_1L(x,0)$, $\chi/\|\chi\|$ is $L(x,0)$ up to phase.
Using $\lceil y\rceil\le y+1$ and $\kappa/\delta\ge1$ gives $\lceil2K\kappa/\delta\rceil+2\le2K\kappa/\delta+3\le(2K+3)\kappa/\delta$.

label: lem:qlsp-walk-circuit
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $B=R\operatorname{diag}(I,O)\Pi$ and $\widetilde B=\operatorname{diag}(B,B)\Pi_Q$, with
$\Sigma=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&\widetilde B\\\widetilde B^\dagger&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Since $\Pi$, $\Pi_Q$, and $\operatorname{diag}(I,O)$ are Hermitian,
block multiplication gives $E=\Pi_1\otimes\Sigma$.

The matrices $R$, $\operatorname{diag}(I,O)$, $\Pi$, $\Pi_1$, and $\Pi_Q$ are Hermitian involutions.
For $R$, this follows from $R_{1,0}R_{0,1}+R_{0,1}R_{1,0}=0$ and $((1-f)/\alpha)^2+(f/\alpha)^2=1$, and for $\Pi_Q$, from $Q_0$ being an
orthogonal projector. Hence, $B$ and $\widetilde B$ are unitary, and $\Sigma$ and $E$ are Hermitian involutions. Put $V_1=|0\rangle\otimes V$ and
$V_2=|0\rangle\otimes V_1$, so that $L=|0\rangle\otimes I_2\otimes V_2$, $V_1^\dagger V_1=I$,
and $V_1Q_bV_1^\dagger=Q_0$. Since $\Pi_QV_2=(Q_0V_1,(I-Q_0)V_1)$,
$V_2^\dagger\widetilde BV_2=V_1^\dagger BQ_0V_1=V_1^\dagger BV_1\,Q_b$.
Moreover, $\Pi V_1=(V,V)/\sqrt2$ gives
$\operatorname{diag}(I,O)\Pi V_1=(V,OV)/\sqrt2$, so the first block row of $R$, $V^\dagger V=I$, and $V^\dagger OV=A$ give
$V_1^\dagger BV_1=((1-f)I+fA)/(\sqrt2\,\alpha)$. Since $\langle0|\Pi_1|0\rangle=1/2$ and $(1-f)I+fA$ is Hermitian,
\begin{align*}
 L^\dagger EL
 &=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}0&V_1^\dagger BV_1Q_b\\Q_bV_1^\dagger B^\dagger V_1&0\end{pmatrix}\\
 &=\frac1{2\sqrt2\,\alpha}\begin{pmatrix}0&((1-f)I+fA)Q_b\\Q_b((1-f)I+fA)&0\end{pmatrix}
 =\frac{H(f)}{2\sqrt2\,\alpha},
\end{align*}
by definition of $H(f)$.

The matrices $B$, $\widetilde B$, $\Sigma$, and $E$ depend linearly on $R$, giving the identity for $E$ in (2). At $f=0,1$, respectively, $E=E_{1,0},E_{0,1}$, so both are Hermitian involutions, and they anticommute because $E=(E_{1,0}+E_{0,1})/\sqrt2$ at $f=1/2$ is an
involution, so $I=E^2=I+\tfrac12(E_{1,0}E_{0,1}+E_{0,1}E_{1,0})$. Put
$u=(1-f)/\alpha$, $v=f/\alpha$, so $E=uE_{1,0}+vE_{0,1}$, and
$X=-vE_{1,0}+uE_{0,1}$. Since $u^2+v^2=1$, $E^2=X^2=I$ and $EX+XE=0$.
Thus, for real $x,y$, $(xE+yX)^2=(x^2+y^2)I$, and $\|M\|^2=\|M^2\|$ for Hermitian $M$ gives
$\|xE+yX\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. Differentiating in $f$ gives $du/df=-f/\alpha^3=-v/\alpha^2$, $dv/df=(1-f)/\alpha^3=u/\alpha^2$, and
$d\alpha^2/df=2(2f-1)$, so
\[
 \frac{dE}{df}=\frac{X}{\alpha^2},\qquad
 \frac{dX}{df}=-\frac{E}{\alpha^2},\qquad
 \frac{d^2E}{df^2}=-\frac{2(2f-1)}{\alpha^4}X-\frac1{\alpha^4}E .
\]
By the norm identity, $\|dE/df\|=\alpha^{-2}$ and, with $(2f-1)^2=2\alpha^2-1$,
$\|d^2E/df^2\|^2=(8\alpha^2-3)/\alpha^8\le16/(3\alpha^4)$, because
$16\alpha^4-24\alpha^2+9=(4\alpha^2-3)^2$. Since $2LL^\dagger-I$ is a reflection,
$\|\frac{d}{df}W\|\le\alpha^{-2}$ and $\|\frac{d^2}{df^2}W\|\le\tfrac4{\sqrt3}\alpha^{-2}$, and the chain rule $W'=f'\frac{dW}{df}$ and $W''=f''\frac{dW}{df}+f'^2\frac{d^2W}{df^2}$ gives
the second claim.

Finally, put $Z_1=\operatorname{diag}(I,0)$ and $Z_2=\operatorname{diag}(Q_0,I-Q_0)$, so
$I_2\otimes\operatorname{diag}(Z_1,Z_2)$ is $Z$ in the block order of $\Sigma$.
Since $Q_0(I-Q_0)=0$,
\[
 Z_1\widetilde B=\begin{pmatrix}BQ_0&B(I-Q_0)\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=\widetilde BZ_2,
\]
and taking adjoints gives $Z_2\widetilde B^\dagger=\widetilde B^\dagger Z_1$, so
$\operatorname{diag}(Z_1,Z_2)$ commutes with $\Sigma$ and $Z$ commutes with $E=\Pi_1\otimes\Sigma$.
Since $Z_1V_2=V_2$ and $Z_2V_2=(Q_0V_1,0)=(V_1Q_b,0)=V_2Q_b$,
$ZL=L\operatorname{diag}(I,Q_b)$. Since $\operatorname{diag}(I,Q_b)$ is Hermitian,
$ZLL^\dagger=L\operatorname{diag}(I,Q_b)L^\dagger=(ZLL^\dagger)^\dagger=LL^\dagger Z$, so $Z$
commutes with $2LL^\dagger-I$, hence with $W(s)$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:qlsp-walk-constants}
Let $\kappa>1$, let $r$, $f$, and $\alpha=\alpha(f(s))$ be as in \Cref{cor:qlsp-walk,def:qlsp-walk-construction}, and,
with $a=1+r=\sqrt\kappa$ and $\omega=2(1+r)^2/(r+2)$, put
\[
 p(s)=\frac{3a\omega}{(1+rs)^4},\qquad
 g(s)=\frac{\beta}{\alpha(1+rs)^2},\qquad \beta=\frac1{2\sqrt2}.
\]
Evaluate the Bernoulli majorant derivative $\mathcal B'$ (\Cref{def:exponential-operators}) and unit-step coefficients $c_0$, $c_1$, and $c_2$ (\Cref{def:unit-coefficients}) at $5\pi/3$, and set
\[
 \rho_1=\frac{5\pi}3,\qquad \rho_2=\frac{5\pi}9\Bigl(7+\frac8{\sqrt3}+8\mathcal B'\Bigr),\qquad
 K=\frac{4\rho_1+6\rho_2}{\beta^2}+\frac{28\sqrt2\,\rho_1^2}{\beta^3}
 +4c_0\rho_1+16c_1\rho_1^2+6c_2\rho_2 .
\]
Let $\Lambda$ be a $C^2$ Hermitian path on an open interval containing $[0,1]$ with
\[
 \|\Lambda'\|\le\frac{\rho_1|f'|}{\alpha^2},\qquad
 \|\Lambda''\|\le\frac{\rho_1(|f''|+\tfrac4{\sqrt3}|f'|^2)}{\alpha^2}
 +\frac{\rho_1(1+2\mathcal B')|f'|^2}{\alpha^4} .
\]
\begin{enumerate}
\item On $[0,1]$, $\|\Lambda'\|\le\rho_1f'/\alpha^2\le4\rho_1a$ and
$\|\Lambda''\|\le\rho_2p/\alpha^2\le12\rho_2a^2$.
\item The Jansen--Ruskai--Seiler coefficient $J_1$ \eqref{eq:jrs-coefficient} of the envelopes $\rho_1f'/\alpha^2$,
$\rho_2p/\alpha^2$, and the gap $g$
is at most $\bigl((4\rho_1+6\rho_2)/\beta^2+28\sqrt2\,\rho_1^2/\beta^3\bigr)a^2$.
\item If $\Lambda(s)$ has spectral width at most $5\pi/3$ on $[0,1]$, then, for every integer $T\ge1$, with $U_\Lambda$ the evolution of $\Lambda(t/T)$,
\[
 \bigl\|e^{-i\Lambda((T-1)/T)}\cdots e^{-i\Lambda(0)}-e^{i\Lambda(1)/2}U_\Lambda(T)e^{-i\Lambda(0)/2}\bigr\|
 \le\frac{(4c_0\rho_1+16c_1\rho_1^2+6c_2\rho_2)a^2}{T}.
\]
Adding $J_1/T$ from (2) gives at most $Ka^2/T$.
\item At width $5\pi/3$,
$\mathcal B'\le6.6027$, $c_0\le0.6538$, $c_1\le0.3577$, $c_2\le0.4872$, and
$K<3.1\cdot10^4$.
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
Differentiating $f$ gives $f'=\omega(1+rs)^{-3}$ and
$|f''|=3r\omega(1+rs)^{-4}\le p$. The bounds $1\le a\le\omega=2a^2/(a+1)\le2a$ give $f'^2/p=\omega/[3a(1+rs)^2]\le2/3$ for $s\ge0$, and $\alpha^2=2(f-1/2)^2+1/2\ge1/2$. Hence, $\|\Lambda'\|\le\rho_1f'/\alpha^2\le2\rho_1f'$ and, with
$\alpha^{-4}\le2\alpha^{-2}$,
\[
 \|\Lambda''\|\le\frac{\rho_1}{\alpha^2}\Bigl(|f''|+\Bigl(\frac4{\sqrt3}+2+4\mathcal B'\Bigr)f'^2\Bigr)
 \le\frac{\rho_1p}{\alpha^2}\Bigl(1+\frac23\Bigl(\frac4{\sqrt3}+2+4\mathcal B'\Bigr)\Bigr)
 =\frac{\rho_2p}{\alpha^2}\le2\rho_2p
\]
for $s\in[0,1]$, where $f'$ and $p$ decrease from $f'(0)=\omega\le2a$ and $p(0)=3a\omega\le6a^2$.

For $J_1$,
$\alpha^2g^2=\beta^2(1+rs)^{-4}$, $f'/(\alpha^2g^2)=\omega(1+rs)/\beta^2$, $p/(\alpha^2g^2)=3a\omega/\beta^2$, and $f'^2/(\alpha^4g^3)=\omega^2/(\beta^3\alpha)$. Integrating over $[0,1]$ gives
\begin{align*}
 J_1&=\frac{\rho_1f'(0)}{\alpha(f(0))^2g(0)^2}+\frac{\rho_1f'(1)}{\alpha(f(1))^2g(1)^2}
 +\int_0^1\left(\frac{\rho_2p}{\alpha^2g^2}+\frac{7\rho_1^2f'^2}{\alpha^4g^3}\right)\,ds\\
 &=\frac{\rho_1\omega(2+r)+3\rho_2a\omega}{\beta^2}+\frac{7\rho_1^2\omega^2}{\beta^3}\int_0^1\frac{ds}\alpha\\
 &\le\Bigl(\frac{4\rho_1+6\rho_2}{\beta^2}+\frac{28\sqrt2\,\rho_1^2}{\beta^3}\Bigr)a^2,
\end{align*}
where the inequality uses $\omega\le2a$, $2+r\le2a$, and $1/\alpha\le\sqrt2$. Substituting the bounds $4\rho_1a$ on $\|\Lambda'\|$ and $6\rho_2a^2$ on $\|\Lambda''\|/2$ into \Cref{thm:unit-steps} and using $a\le a^2$ gives (3).

Finally, $\sum_{k\ge1}|B_{2k}|w^{2k}/(2k)!=1-\tfrac w2\cot\tfrac w2$ gives the closed form
$\mathcal B(w)=2+\tfrac w2-\tfrac w2\cot\tfrac w2$, while $\mathcal N(w)=(1-\tfrac w2\cot\tfrac w2)/w^2$ by definition.
Put $\mathcal C(w)=\tfrac12+w\mathcal N(w)=(\mathcal B(w)-1)/w$, so that $\mathcal C'=\mathcal N+w\mathcal N'$. At
$w=5\pi/3$, where $\cot\tfrac w2=-\sqrt3$ and $\sin^2\tfrac w2=\tfrac14$, evaluation and differentiation give
\[
 \mathcal B'=\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2+\frac{5\pi}3,\qquad
 \mathcal C=\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2+\frac3{5\pi},\qquad
 \mathcal C'=1-\frac9{25\pi^2}.
\]
The bounds $3.14159<\pi<3.14160$ and $1.73205<\sqrt3<1.73206$ give $\mathcal B'\le6.6027$, $1.55\le\mathcal C\le1.55702$, and
$\mathcal C'\le0.96353$. Substituting these into $\mathcal N=(\mathcal C-1/2)/w$ and $\mathcal N'=(\mathcal C'-\mathcal N)/w$ gives $0.2005\le\mathcal N\le0.2019$ and $\mathcal N'\le0.1458$, and substitution into $c_0=1/4+2\mathcal N$, $c_1=1/64+\mathcal N/4+2\mathcal N'$, and $c_2=1/12+2\mathcal N$ gives the three bounds. The definitions, these bounds, and $1.41421<\sqrt2<1.41422$ give $\rho_1\le5.236$, $\rho_2\le112.5$, and $\beta\ge0.35355$. Each term of $K$ increases with its nonnegative numerator factors and decreases with $\beta$, so
\[
 K\le\frac{4\cdot5.236+6\cdot112.5}{0.35355^2}+\frac{28\cdot1.4143\cdot5.236^2}{0.35355^3}
 +4\cdot0.6538\cdot5.236+16\cdot0.3577\cdot5.236^2+6\cdot0.4872\cdot112.5<3.1\cdot10^4 .
\]
